If there are folk starving in the woods, our granary holds plenty of xi wheat, and Gujia does not turn away an empty belly when our own pots are full. But I will not send my people wandering into the trees carrying heavy sacks for ghosts or a name from a shadow. Tell me which path leads to their hearths, or let them send a runner to our clearing, and we will talk of bread.

Peace to you, shadow of the night. 

You speak of a people named Wewush, but our scouts have walked many days along the shore and through the trees, and we have met no such folk. Our granary is full of golden wheat, it is true, and the earth has been generous to Ilkei. We do not turn away the hungry, nor do we hoard when bellies pinch, but a chief cannot send good grain out into the mist after a name spoken only in sleep. 

Tell me, spirit—where do these folk kindle their fires? Which way does the path run, and who leads them? If they are flesh and bone, let them send a walker to our hearth, or show me the true trail under the sun, and we will weigh what we can share. Until then, my people’s grain stays beneath the roof we built for it.

Tell me where their fires burn, spirit, or let them send their own living envoys to our huts. Until then, my people’s harvest stays beneath our own roof.

You speak of a place called Joawethom, shadow, but my people have walked the shores and marshes for twenty years and met no one by that name. If there are folk starving there, where do their fires burn? How many days must a man carry a pack to find their tents, and what paths do they tread? 

We have grain in our bins because our hands cleared the stone and dug the ditches, not because smoke whispered in the night. If living men come to our borders with open hands, we will deal fairly with them, as is our way. Until flesh and blood stand before me in the daylight, my wheat stays where it keeps dry. Tell me where this Joawethom lies, or leave my sleep to the wind.

Otherwise, let me rest; the morning brings work that needs waking hands, not sleeping words.

I do not know any people called Wewush, spirit of the night. Our wanderers walked many days and found empty shores, salt water, and thick woods, but no other fires burning under the sky. 

If these strangers truly live, where do their lodges stand, and why have they sent no men of flesh to ask of our elders face to face? Joawethom does not cast the sweat of its fields into the dark for a phantom name. Tell me who they are and where their smoke rises, or leave my sleep, for words carried on the wind fill no empty bellies and bind no kin.

Our bins hold plenty of grain, true enough, and Wewush does not turn away hungry folk who come to our fires. But I will not send good wheat into the empty brush on the word of a night shadow. 

Tell me plainly: where do these people dwell, how many days' walk from our shore, and what path leads to their hearths? If their bellies are truly empty, let flesh-and-blood runners show themselves by daylight, and we will talk of fair trade. Until then, the grain stays in the granary.
